lead: The coffee or green tea ritual is a daily habit of drinking caffeinated beverages, often in the morning, as part of a routine for looking fresher and less puffy. Practitioners say the drinks help them look more awake and, in the case of green tea, supply polyphenols such as EGCG that they associate with healthy-looking skin.[1][2]

Both drinks contain caffeine, which blocks adenosine receptors and relieves sleepiness. Large single doses can briefly raise urine output in people who have gone without caffeine, while regular users develop tolerance to that effect.[2] Green tea also contains polyphenols including EGCG; Wikipedia notes that a 2011 European Food Safety Authority panel found most claimed benefits of green tea lacked sufficient scientific support.[1]

Looks-focused communities discuss caffeine in both directions: some see coffee as a tool for leanness and energy, while others link it to skin, sleep and growth concerns. Research on caffeine and sleep is extensive, and sleep is a factor people connect with how rested they look.[3][4]

angle.text: People drink coffee or green tea in the morning to look more awake and to reduce the puffy look they associate with water retention. Green tea drinkers add that its polyphenols fit a skin-friendly diet.

paras: The ritual usually means a cup of coffee or green tea at the start of the day. Brewed green tea is almost entirely water, with caffeine and polyphenols such as EGCG and other catechins; supplements and extracts can contain much higher concentrations, up to about 17 percent caffeine by weight in some extracts.[1]

Proponents point to caffeine's alertness effect and to its short-lived diuretic action as reasons the habit might leave the face looking less swollen in the morning. Caffeine's diuretic effect is documented for large doses in people not accustomed to it, and tolerance develops with regular use.[2]

Caffeine's structure resembles adenosine, so it occupies adenosine receptors without activating them, which temporarily relieves drowsiness; the A2A receptor appears central to the wakefulness effect.[2] In the kidney, receptor blockade increases water and salt excretion after large single doses.[2]

No studies found on drinking coffee or green tea as a routine for facial puffiness or facial appearance. Research on the drinks themselves covers general health outcomes: a BMJ umbrella review summarised meta-analyses of coffee consumption across many health outcomes,[5] and Wikipedia reports small blood pressure reductions and modest LDL cholesterol lowering from green tea in trials, including a 2013 Cochrane review, with no good evidence for weight loss.[1]

Sleep has been studied closely. A 2023 meta-analysis of 24 studies found that caffeine reduced total sleep time by about 45 minutes and sleep efficiency by 7 percent, and lengthened sleep onset by about 9 minutes.[3] A 2017 systematic review reported that caffeine typically prolonged sleep latency and worsened perceived sleep quality.[4]

EFSA considers intake up to 400 mg of caffeine per day safe for non-pregnant adults and up to 200 mg per day for pregnant and breastfeeding women. Even around 100 mg per day can disrupt sleep in some people without tolerance.[2]

High-dose green tea extract, mainly through EGCG, has been linked to liver damage. EFSA found long-term intake above 800 mg EGCG per day raised liver enzymes in some people, regards traditionally brewed tea as safe with rare liver injury, and in 2017 Health Canada recommended a warning label for extracts.[1]

timeline.event: EFSA panel reviews health claims for green tea, finding most lacked sufficient support.[1]
Cochrane review of green tea reports modest blood pressure and LDL cholesterol reductions.[1]

lore.intro: Coffee shows up in looksmaxxing forums as a leanmaxxing and energy aid and, in other threads, as something that may harm skin, sleep or growth.

claims.believers: Threads on looksmax.org such as one titled 'coffee is so good for leanmaxxing' present caffeine as an appetite and energy aid for getting leaner.[6]
claims.experts: A 2023 pilot study examined coffee and tea consumption and weight control in adolescents,[7] and Wikipedia reports no good evidence that green tea aids weight loss.[1]

claims.claim: Coffee is good for the thyroid.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread titled 'coffee is very good for your thyroid' argues it supports thyroid function.[8]
claims.experts: A systematic review of levothyroxine interactions notes that coffee and other beverages can alter absorption of thyroid medication.[9]

claims.believers: Threads titled 'does coffee stunt your growth' and 'could coffee stunt my growth' show users asking whether caffeine affects height.[10][11]
claims.experts: None of the sources reviewed here address caffeine and height; no study cited on this page has tested it.

claims.claim: Coffee dehydrates and ages facial skin.
claims.believers: Some looksmax.org posters argue caffeine dehydrates the face and works against skincare.
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that the diuretic effect applies to large doses in people without caffeine tolerance, and that regular users do not show increased urine output.[2]

name: Coffee / green tea ritual

card.summary: Caffeine drinks used as a de-puffing routine; no study has tested the face effect.
card.note: Caffeine affects sleep; high-dose tea extracts linked to liver injury.

quick.overview:
People drink coffee or green tea as a daily ritual intended to reduce puffiness.

Caffeine has a short-lived diuretic effect in non-habitual users, but no published trial has tested these drinks for facial appearance.
quick.mechanism: Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors and may increase urine output briefly; tolerance develops with regular use [2].
quick.risks: Caffeine can disrupt sleep. Concentrated green tea extracts have been associated with liver toxicity [1][2].
